newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Yen rally puts brakes on carry plays.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Yen rally puts brakes on carry plays.

text.p: The yen's latest rally against the dollar threatens a reversal of fortune for bond traders who have enjoyed an easy ride on yen leverage, analysts said on Tuesday.

Investors should lighten up on dollar assets and embark on a neutral stance on Japan. But with yields on Japanese Government Bonds (JGB) still meagre, a straight leap from Treasuries was seen too risky.
"If you are significantly underweight (Japan), you should be moving back to neutral," said Stephen Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International in London.

Though the currency backdrop has now moved to more in favour of yen bonds, the prospect of an interest rate rise in Japan later this year means Treasuries will continue to outshine Japan, at least in the medium term, economists said.

The yen burst higher on Monday, setting a six month high of 111.80 to the dollar on a hunch that data out on Wednesday might show Japan's trade surplus swelling in April. At 1229 GMT, dollar/yen was quoted at 112.44/49.

"There is no reason for me to panic at this point," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London. "But if you get below 100 and the Japanese authorities don't make an attempt to defend that level than that could change the ball game a lot."
IBJ's Hannah saw the pain barrier for yen carry positions at 110. "Obviously the (yen's) trend has reversed," he said, but the yen was unlikely to break above 110.

Japan's slack economy and rock-bottom interest rates in the past two years has enabled traders to enjoy the twin benefit of borrowing cheaply in yen and picking up higher yields elsewhere, especially in U.S. Treasuries.
But with the Japanese economy now emerging from the doldrums, investors should review their yen portfolios, analysts said, but not aggressively.

"If you're going to get some reduction in dollar bond holdings you would look for a rally in dollar/yen back up towards 115-116," said Marshall, adding that there would be more concern if the U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates in July.
Some traders have dabbled in the short end of the JGB curve as a vehicle to gain exposure to yen, but the longer end is regarded an expensive bet.
"At 2.5 percent the benchmark yield is not terribly attractive," Hannah said. "A lot of people think we'll be going through three percent this year."

The benchmark 182nd cash JGB was yielding 2.490 percent in afternoon European trade. The September JGB future contract on LIFFE stood at 123.23, up from 123.14 in Tokyo when it shed earlier gains after weaker-than-expected April machinery orders.

Analysts said the spotlight was now on the Tankan survey on June 24 for rate guidelines. Although some growth is almost certain to emerge, the survey is likely to show the economy is not out of the woods yet, analysts said.
In the U.S., retail sales data due on Thursday may set the near term tone for the bond market, they said.
Marshall of Chase forecast the 10-year JGB/Treasury yield spread to narrow by 50 basis points in the second quarter of this year from 396 basis points at present.
Neil Williams, chief economist at Sumitomo Finance International in London said the yen rally was temporary given the cautious attitude of the Bank of Japan towards rate hikes.
"Once people realise that a tightening is not imminent and when it comes it's won't be aggressive, the yen will trade back," he said.
